- A SiC face vocabulary beyond Si, C and a: (03-38) is written here as `4H_SiC_03-38_face`, a new word no program or ontology entry knows. Faces should be Miller indices (with polytype and off-cut), so a program can say which it has constants for and the runtime can refuse a misspelling. *([Yano et al. 2002](/writing/interface-study-yano-2002))*
- The interface-state program's energies should be the sample's to choose (`OBSERVE Dit AT Ec-0.15 eV`), or the program should report the whole curve it can support; today only 0.3, 0.4 and 0.5 eV exist, and this paper's result lies at 0.1 to 0.2 eV. *([Yano et al. 2002](/writing/interface-study-yano-2002))*
- The sic_interface_states program returns nothing (not even a refusal with a reason) when a history has no dry-oxygen step. A wet history should be refused with a stated reason, so the page can say why, rather than appear as “no program”. *([Yano et al. 2002](/writing/interface-study-yano-2002))*
- In situ steps: a statement that two RUNs are in the same tube with no unload between them (`IN_SITU`), against Kobayashi's anneal in another furnace (a transfer through air). Here the argon anneal is in situ, and the gas switch in between is an unknown we had to write as an extra step. *([Yano et al. 2002](/writing/interface-study-yano-2002))*
- The measurement temperature and method on an observable (`MEASURE Dit METHOD conductance AT 300 K`; C-V at 100 K): the same sample gives different counts of shallow states by method and temperature, which is how this paper argues. *([Yano et al. 2002](/writing/interface-study-yano-2002))*
- OFFCUT read by the SiC growth program (constants per face and off-cut). Song's Si face is on axis, Goto and Hijikata's is 8° off, this chapter's is unrecorded, and the Si-face constants do not transfer between them (28 to 64% low here). The field exists on samples and no program reads it. *([Gupta and Akhtar 2011](/writing/interface-study-gupta-akhtar))*
- A ramp rate as a statement (`RAMP RATE 5 C/min FROM 800 TO 1150`), so the chapter's stated rate is written as the paper gives it, not as a duration we derive. *([Gupta and Akhtar 2011](/writing/interface-study-gupta-akhtar))*
- The sic_growth program's scope check labels a history outside its tested scope whenever any step is not dry oxygen, so a load and ramp in nitrogen, which grows nothing, marks every number here “outside the tested scope”. The check should look only at the steps that grow oxide. *([Gupta and Akhtar 2011](/writing/interface-study-gupta-akhtar))*
- Bubbler temperature as an ambient statement (`H2O FROM bubbler AT 85 C`) that the runtime turns into a water partial pressure, so a wet recipe is written as the paper states it rather than as our computed mixture. *([Gupta and Akhtar 2011](/writing/interface-study-gupta-akhtar))*
- A cumulative or replicate series: `REPLICATES 4` on a measurement, so the four samples per point are part of the record (and their scatter, if a paper gives it, becomes the tolerance). *([Gupta and Akhtar 2011](/writing/interface-study-gupta-akhtar))*
- A grid whose length is a state (`GRID oxide { FROM: 0; TO: x_ox; CELLS: 50 }`), or a stretched coordinate with position-dependent velocity, so interstitial and oxidant profiles can live in the growing oxide. This is the one change that would let the Si and C emission model be written as a candidate structure beside the linear-parabolic law. *([Goto and Hijikata 2016](/writing/interface-study-goto-2016))*
- `integral(expr)` over a product of fields (the paper's ∫ κ C_Si C_O dx), not only `integral(F)` of one field. *([Goto and Hijikata 2016](/writing/interface-study-goto-2016))*
- A growth rate against thickness as an observable (`OBSERVE rate OF x_ox AT Thickness`), so in-situ rate data can be scored directly instead of integrated into times that carry every reading error. *([Goto and Hijikata 2016](/writing/interface-study-goto-2016))*
- A time origin at gas admission and an observation that starts later (`MEASURE … FROM first_resolved_thickness`): the paper's clock starts when argon is replaced by oxygen, its data at 3 to 13 nm; we had to anchor the clock with the program's own constants. *([Goto and Hijikata 2016](/writing/interface-study-goto-2016))*
- OFFCUT read by the growth program: this Si face is 8° off axis, Song's on axis, and Song's Si-face constants are up to 36% slow here. The C face is 0.5° off. *([Goto and Hijikata 2016](/writing/interface-study-goto-2016))*
- The sic_growth scope check marks a history outside its tested scope when any step is not dry oxygen, including an argon heat-up that grows nothing. It should check only the steps where oxide grows (and the temperatures of those). *([Goto and Hijikata 2016](/writing/interface-study-goto-2016))*
- **Nitric oxide (and N2O, NH3) as gases.** The NO anneal at 1200 °C for 70 min is a stated step the language cannot write; it is an EVENT here. `mix:NO=1.0` would let it be simulated by a program that reads `p_NO` (nitrogen at the interface, Figure 9; the interface-state reduction, Figure 6). *([Li, Luo and Ye 2023](/writing/interface-study-li-2023))*
- **An implant statement.** `IMPLANT P ENERGY 30 keV DOSE 1e13 [THROUGH FieldOxide]` as a history step, carrying the species, the projected range and the damage a program can read. The paper's central variable is a sample field no program reads. *([Li, Luo and Ye 2023](/writing/interface-study-li-2023))*
- **A profile observable with the instrument in it.** The composition target has no observation form: an `OBSERVATION_MODEL` returns one number. A profile result (value against position from the interface) and a reduction such as `convolve(F, w)` with a stated probe width, sampled at positions, would let Figure 8 be scored and would separate the instrument from the interface. *([Li, Luo and Ye 2023](/writing/interface-study-li-2023))*
- **A grid whose length follows a state** (the oxide thickness), so a surface sink sits at the surface while the oxide grows; today the candidate program's sink is at a fixed 60 nm and its carbon is an upper bound. *([Li, Luo and Ye 2023](/writing/interface-study-li-2023))*
- **OFFCUT read by programs.** The 4° off-cut is recorded and ignored; it sets the step density that roughens the interface the EDS line crosses, and Song's constants are on axis. *([Li, Luo and Ye 2023](/writing/interface-study-li-2023))*
- **A rate observable, measured at a thickness, not at a time.** The chapter's data are dX/dt against X. The language observes states at the end of a history, so the rate had to be integrated to thickness against a reconstructed time with an unknown time zero. An observation of a state's time derivative (`EQUATION: Growth_rate = d(x_ox)/dt`) and a result indexed by a state (`MEASURE Growth_rate AT Thickness = 1.0e-6`) would compare the rates directly and need no time zero; it would also have answered “is the initial rate enhanced?” in one row. *([Hijikata, Yagi, Yaguchi and Yoshida 2013](/writing/interface-study-hijikata-2013))*
- **A measurement during a RUN** (`MEASURE <observable> DURING <run> EVERY <s>` or in situ), so an in-situ ellipsometry run is one history with many measured points instead of a curve sampled by re-running the history to each time. *([Hijikata, Yagi, Yaguchi and Yoshida 2013](/writing/interface-study-hijikata-2013))*
- **Clock reference** (as for Song 2004): `TIME_ZERO at_gas_on | at_first_point`, so an in-situ run's time axis can be stated rather than searched. *([Hijikata, Yagi, Yaguchi and Yoshida 2013](/writing/interface-study-hijikata-2013))*
- **Predictor: a thin-oxide channel in the SiC growth program**, with its own pressure law. The Si and C emission model is writable today: FIELDs for Si and C interstitials and oxygen in the oxide on a grid travelling with the interface, FLUX with D_Si, D_C, D_O, BOUNDARY fluxes ν_Si k C_O, ν_C k C_O and (2 − ν_Si − ν_C − α/2) k C_O at the interface (Eq. 10), an OxideGrowth rate k0 (1 − left(C_Si)/C_Si⁰)(1 − left(C_C)/C_C⁰) C_O / N0 (Eq. 8). Table 1 gives the oxide-side constants; ν_Si, ν_C and k0 per face and temperature exist only as points on Figure 6, so they would be graph reads. Its grid would need to follow the growing oxide (no grid of varying length today). *([Hijikata, Yagi, Yaguchi and Yoshida 2013](/writing/interface-study-hijikata-2013))*
- **Predictor: the program scales its whole rate by p_O2.** Hijikata's initial rate R_r is nearly independent of pressure while R_g is proportional (Figure 8). Any SiC program used for low-pressure or ramp-in-diluted-oxygen histories needs the two separated. *([Hijikata, Yagi, Yaguchi and Yoshida 2013](/writing/interface-study-hijikata-2013))*
- **One oxide per history, from a growth law for the gas.** Two programs grow 134 and 37 nm on the same 150 min history (59 nm measured); the inventory's germanium dose follows its own oxide. The predictor should take one oxide thickness (or a stated one: `MEASURED_OXIDE_NM` as an input, as done for the nanowire program's RUN_FLAT_OXIDE_NM) and feed it to every composition program. With the stated oxide the inventory program's width is a prediction of Long's profiles with nothing grown. *([Long et al. 2012](/writing/interface-study-long-2012))*
- **A dry-oxygen SiGe growth program, or a refusal.** The Rabie program runs dry histories at its wet 800 °C constants and labels them “direction only”. Long gives eleven dry oxide thicknesses at 800 to 1000 °C on two compositions; they would fit or test one. *([Long et al. 2012](/writing/interface-study-long-2012))*
- **STARTING_OXIDE_NM read by the SiGe programs.** The native oxide is 5 nm here (a quarter of the 25 min oxide), and it carries GeO2 (XPS). Neither SiGe program reads it. *([Long et al. 2012](/writing/interface-study-long-2012))*
- **Layered sample with a finite alloy.** `LAYER SiGe { COMPOSITION: Si0.85Ge0.15; THICKNESS: 80 nm } on LAYER Si { THICKNESS: 100 nm }`: needed to say when the pile-up consumes the layer (Long's Figure 6 at 150 min, and his Eq. 8). *([Long et al. 2012](/writing/interface-study-long-2012))*
- **An observation model for the instrument's depth resolution.** RBS and XPS report a profile smoothed by about 5 nm (estimated here from the un-oxidized edge) and 3.5 or 11.7 nm (Ge2p, Ge3d). A statement such as `OBSERVATION_MODEL ... RESOLUTION gaussian 5 nm` would let a sharp predicted profile be compared with a measured one without the hand-written smoothing in this study file. *([Long et al. 2012](/writing/interface-study-long-2012))*
- **A depth profile as a target.** Results are scalars at chosen depths (10 nm, 30 nm). Long's data are profiles with the front aligned at zero by the authors; a profile target (depth series, with the front position as an unknown) would score the whole shape. *([Long et al. 2012](/writing/interface-study-long-2012))*
- **The conserved dose in the inventory program.** Its comment follows Long's Eq. 7 (the germanium of the consumed alloy, x N_ox X/(1−X)) but places that dose as the excess above X in an exponential. Counting atoms with the alloy shrinking by the silicon removed gives an excess of x N_ox X, as scripts/analyse_germanium_inventory.py already uses. The program's width is 1/(1−X) too large: 18% at X = 0.15, 100% at X = 0.5. A predictor change, not a language one; it is listed here because this paper is its source. *([Long et al. 2012](/writing/interface-study-long-2012))*
- **A clean word for “native oxide not removed”.** The CLEAN vocabulary has no entry for an uncleaned surface; not_stated is wrong here, because the paper does state it. *([Long et al. 2012](/writing/interface-study-long-2012))*
- **Interface-resident species and operators that act along an interface.** A `FIELD` on an interface (surface concentration of mobile germanium) with `Transport` along it, a source tied to the oxidation flux, and an exchange into the crystal below. Without it, the paper's mechanism and every one of its 14 measured lengths and widths cannot be written. *([Thornton et al. 2022](/writing/interface-study-thornton-2022))*
- **A second spatial coordinate, or a sidewall coordinate.** `GRID` is one-dimensional and travels with a planar front; a fin needs height along the sidewall and lateral depth. *([Thornton et al. 2022](/writing/interface-study-thornton-2022))*
- **SHAPE read by every program, with a refusal.** The SiGe programs check only nanosheet and nanowire; a SHAPE: fin sample is run as a planar alloy without a label. Every program should state which shapes it accepts and label the rest outside its scope. *([Thornton et al. 2022](/writing/interface-study-thornton-2022))*
- **Layered samples.** `LAYER` blocks (composition, thickness, strain) for a superlattice on a silicon base, so that a program knows each SiGe layer holds 15 nm of alloy. *([Thornton et al. 2022](/writing/interface-study-thornton-2022))*
- **A contour observable.** `OBSERVATION_MODEL ... EQUATION: L = extent(x_Ge > 0.03 along sidewall)`: an observable defined by a level of a field. *([Thornton et al. 2022](/writing/interface-study-thornton-2022))*
- **Residual gas of a sealed ampule.** The ambient was written as air at 35 mtorr; a statement for “sealed, pumped to P, gas unknown” with the oxygen partial pressure as an unknown (`VARY p_O2`) would let alignment search it. *([Thornton et al. 2022](/writing/interface-study-thornton-2022))*
- **Sidewall orientation.** ORIENTATION is a wafer property; a fin's sidewall plane is a separate property that the growth programs should read. *([Thornton et al. 2022](/writing/interface-study-thornton-2022))*
- **Which step is the oxidation.** A lamp heat-up written in oxygen, as an RTP usually runs, makes the trap-density program read the oxidation temperature as 25 °C and refuse every history here; the heat-up had to be written in vacuum, which removes 0.2 to 1.6 nm of oxide the programs would otherwise grow. A `ROLE oxidation|ramp|anneal|pull` on each RUN would let programs find the step by what it is. *([Fukuda et al. 1992](/writing/interface-study-fukuda-1992))*
- **Isotopes and process gases.** Deuterium had to be written as hydrogen (`pure_H2`), silane as nitrogen, and the phosphorus source not at all: the language's gases are Ar, H2, H2O, N2 and O2. `mix:D2=1` and `mix:SiH4=…`, `POCl3` would record what was done; a program could then ignore them, or carry an isotope effect (the paper's SIMS counts deuterium). *([Fukuda et al. 1992](/writing/interface-study-fukuda-1992))*
- **A deposition and a doping as steps.** The 350 nm polysilicon at 620 °C and its 900 °C doping are written as nitrogen holds. A `DEPOSIT polysilicon 350 nm` statement that caps the oxide (no gas reaches it afterwards) would say why the gas does not matter and let a program ask whether hydrogen can leave through the cap, which is what the computed bound below depends on. *([Fukuda et al. 1992](/writing/interface-study-fukuda-1992))*
- **An observation's timing.** The trap density and charge were measured after the gate steps, not after the anneal the figure is about. The language ends the history at the measurement implicitly. An explicit `OBSERVE Dit, Nf AFTER <step>` would make the gap between the anneal and the measurement visible on the page and let a program answer at the anneal as well. *([Fukuda et al. 1992](/writing/interface-study-fukuda-1992))*
- **Thickness and time on separate figures.** Figures 2 and 3 are the same wafers against thickness and against time, never paired. A sample field `OXIDE_NM` read as a measured property beside a stated time would let each wafer carry both, and let a growth program be scored on it without a pairing of ours. *([Fukuda et al. 1992](/writing/interface-study-fukuda-1992))*
- **Where the hydrogen goes.** Not a language gap but a program one the language exposes. Since commit 7f1ec87 the trap-density program's capping has Brower's activation energy and capped sites release hydrogen at 900 °C, but released hydrogen leaves the model: nothing holds the deuterium SIMS finds in the oxide (1.7×10^12 to 2.8×10^13 cm⁻²), so nothing can recap on cooling under the polysilicon, and the 900 °C gate doping erases every anneal. A hydrogen inventory per layer, and a `DEPOSIT` that caps it, would let a program ask what the paper's wafers kept. *([Fukuda et al. 1992](/writing/interface-study-fukuda-1992))*
- **Which step is the oxidation.** Writing the push in oxygen, which may be what was done, makes the trap-density program read the oxidation temperature as 25 °C and refuse. A `ROLE oxidation|load|pull|anneal` on each RUN would let a push be written as the heating it is. *([Kar and Narasimhan 1987](/writing/interface-study-kar-1987))*
- **An etch that removes oxide.** The 1100 °C sacrificial oxide is grown and stripped in HF before the gate oxide; it had to be an event. `ETCH REMOVE ALL` (or `TO <nm>`) after a RUN would let the preoxidation be simulated, so that its heat reaches the programs and its oxide does not. *([Kar and Narasimhan 1987](/writing/interface-study-kar-1987))*
- **Dit(E) as an observable.** The predictor's energy rows are fixed target names written only after hydrogen. An observation `Dit AT_ENERGY <eV> ABOVE Ev BY admittance|quasistatic` with the substrate type would let a paper's distribution be stated as what was measured, and let a program say it cannot answer at that energy rather than be silent. *([Kar and Narasimhan 1987](/writing/interface-study-kar-1987))*
- **Peaks and cross sections.** The paper's central results are a peak's height and energy and a capture cross section against thickness. The ontology has no observable for any of them. *([Kar and Narasimhan 1987](/writing/interface-study-kar-1987))*
- **A device tied to a calibration series.** Each measured device is known by its thickness; its oxidation time comes only from Figure 1. A sample field `OXIDE_NM` read as a measured property, and a way to say a RUN's duration is whatever makes that thickness (an inverse VARY), would replace the times inferred by hand here. *([Kar and Narasimhan 1987](/writing/interface-study-kar-1987))*
- **Doping and gate metal as inputs.** DOPING is recorded and read by no program; here it decides which half of the gap was measured. The gate metal (Au on n-type, Al on p-type) is not recordable; an aluminium gate can release hydrogen at the interface even without an anneal. *([Kar and Narasimhan 1987](/writing/interface-study-kar-1987))*
- **A clean word.** The vocabulary has no `sacrificial_oxide_HF` for “preoxidation was part of the surface cleaning”; CLEAN had to be `not_stated` although the paper states it. *([Kar and Narasimhan 1987](/writing/interface-study-kar-1987))*
- **Ammonia and nitrous oxide as gases.** `AMBIENT mix:NH3=1.0` and `mix:N2O=1.0` are refused (the gases are Ar, H2, H2O, N2, O2). Adding p_NH3 and p_N2O as controls would let a nitridation be written as done; today it can only be written as nitrogen, which carries its heat and nothing else. Every row here would then at least be run on the paper's history. *([Tsai, Wu, Wu and Hu 1987](/writing/interface-study-tsai-1987))*
- **A program for nitrogen at the interface.** With the gas written, a program has to say what it does: incorporate nitrogen at the Si/SiO2 interface (rate rising with temperature, saturating with time), release hydrogen into the film, and shift fixed charge and trap generation. The paper's Table II (more negative flat-band voltage at lower nitridation temperature, positive after 3 h at 1100 and 1150 °C) is the first check such a program would have. *([Tsai, Wu, Wu and Hu 1987](/writing/interface-study-tsai-1987))*
- **An electrical stress step.** Figure 1 and 2 are measured during constant-current injection; the language has no statement for it, so the paper's main result is outside any history. A `STRESS` statement with current density, polarity and fluence, and observables for generated trap density and flat-band shift, would make it a target. *([Tsai, Wu, Wu and Hu 1987](/writing/interface-study-tsai-1987))*
- **The gate as a sample property a program reads.** A flat-band voltage needs the gate work function (As-doped polysilicon here). `GATE` is recorded on the sample and read by nothing; a program computing Vfb from fixed charge, trapped charge and the gate would let Table II be scored. *([Tsai, Wu, Wu and Hu 1987](/writing/interface-study-tsai-1987))*
- **The forming-gas time and H2 fraction (history).** Since 11 November the capping rate has Brower's 1.66 eV (see the Reed 1989 page), so a forming-gas ramp from room temperature counts for little (the cold-furnace ramps lower the density 37%, where they gave ten times before). What still sets the predicted density is what the paper does not state: the forming-gas time (10 to 60 min) and the H2 fraction (5% gives 3.7 times the density of 10%). *([Tsai, Wu, Wu and Hu 1987](/writing/interface-study-tsai-1987))*
- **Process steps that bring hydrogen.** LPCVD polysilicon (silane), CVD oxide and the ammonia itself are hydrogen sources the history records only as events. A hydrogen source on an EVENT or a deposition RUN with its gas would let them reach the trap-density program. *([Tsai, Wu, Wu and Hu 1987](/writing/interface-study-tsai-1987))*
- **Hydrogen release tied to what the history put there (predictor).** The program now releases hydrogen (Si–H → Si• + H at Brower's rate), but a release can only raise the density where an earlier step capped sites, and on this page none can. It also has no release for the second population and does not use the computed Si–H energy against the gas's p_H2. Until the hydrogen sources below can be written, an RTA, a vacuum anneal and a rapid pull still look the same as no step. *([O'Sullivan et al. 2001](/writing/interface-study-osullivan-2001))*
- **Hydrogen brought by a step that is not a gas anneal.** Polysilicon from silane at 620 °C, POCl3 doping, plasma steps and moisture during a slow pull passivate the interface (the paper, PDF p. 9-10). The language records them as EVENTs that do nothing. A `SOURCE hydrogen` clause on a deposition EVENT, or an AMBIENT for a deposition (`mix:SiH4=…`), and a stated moisture on pulls, would let a program see them. The vocabulary of gases is Ar, H2, H2O, N2, O2; silane, POCl3, NH3 and N2O are refused. *([O'Sullivan et al. 2001](/writing/interface-study-osullivan-2001))*
- **Which step is the oxidation.** The RTO heat-up had to be written in nitrogen: the trap-density program takes the oxidation's temperature and time from the first dry-oxygen RUN, so a heat-up in oxygen from 25 °C would be read as an oxidation at 25 °C. A `ROLE oxidation|anneal|ramp|pull` on each RUN (as Hung's page asked) would remove the trap. *([O'Sullivan et al. 2001](/writing/interface-study-osullivan-2001))*
- **A gate on the sample.** Polysilicon, aluminium and a mercury probe behave differently under hydrogen (the paper: lightly doped polysilicon needs a longer alloy). GATE is recorded here as a sample field no program reads. A gate field in the ontology, read by the hydrogen operator as a barrier or a source, would let processes 1-2 and 3-5 differ. *([O'Sullivan et al. 2001](/writing/interface-study-osullivan-2001))*
- **A pull as a speed.** “a pull from the furnace at 600 °C at 8 cm/min” is a speed, not a duration or a cooling rate; the boat travel is unknown. A `PULL SPEED 8 cm/min FROM 600` statement with a furnace profile would turn it into a temperature against time. *([O'Sullivan et al. 2001](/writing/interface-study-osullivan-2001))*
- **A measurement that is a difference.** Table I's peaks are densities after subtracting a background measured on another (hydrogen-passivated) sample. An observation statement naming the reference sample would let such numbers be compared with a difference of two simulations. *([O'Sullivan et al. 2001](/writing/interface-study-osullivan-2001))*
- **An HF dip as a clean.** CLEAN accepts named cleans only; a bare pre-oxidation HF dip (process 3) had to be written not_stated. *([O'Sullivan et al. 2001](/writing/interface-study-osullivan-2001))*
- **A gate that supplies hydrogen.** Reed's Al-gate capacitors anneal at the same rate in any ambient because aluminium reacting with hydroxyl at the Al–SiO2 interface releases atomic hydrogen. The language can record `GATE: Al` on a sample, but no statement says the gate is a hydrogen source during every later heat; an RTA in nitrogen therefore anneals nothing. A sample layer with a declared reservoir (`LAYER Al { SOURCE: H }`) or a `SOURCE H` clause on a RUN would let the Al-gate curves be simulated at all. *([Reed 1989](/writing/interface-study-reed-1989))*
- **Atomic against molecular hydrogen.** Bare oxides anneal much faster in atomic hydrogen than in H2 (PDF p. 3); the language's gases are Ar, H2, H2O, N2 and O2. An `H` species in `mix:` (and a program that reads it) is needed before corona, plasma or post-metal anneals can be written. *([Reed 1989](/writing/interface-study-reed-1989))*
- **A measured starting state.** Every case here starts from an oxidation we invented because the program cannot be told “the sample has 8.4×10^10 cm⁻² eV⁻¹ of traps at t = 0”. A sample field such as `STARTING_DIT: 8.4e10` (as STARTING_OXIDE_NM does for thickness) would let an anneal series be tested on its kinetics alone, without an unknown oxidation in front of it. *([Reed 1989](/writing/interface-study-reed-1989))*
- **One sample measured along an anneal.** Each point of a decay curve is written as a separate history ending at that time. Whether the paper annealed one capacitor repeatedly (with cooling and a measurement between anneals) or a fresh one each time is not stated, and the language cannot say which. A `REPEAT` of anneal-and-measure on one sample, with the cooling between, would make the difference explicit. *([Reed 1989](/writing/interface-study-reed-1989))*
- **A plateau in the trap-density program** (a predictor change). Commit 7f1ec87 added Brower's Arrhenius capping (1.66 eV) and dissociation of Si–H (2.56 eV); the steady state they give is 18 to 110 times below Burte's plateau. Still missing: a floor of sites hydrogen does not cap, or a spread of capping barriers, and a rate level set by data at more than one temperature. *([Reed 1989](/writing/interface-study-reed-1989))*
- **An etch that removes oxide.** The 1100 °C preoxide is grown and stripped before the oxidation that matters. The language has no statement that removes oxide, so the step had to become an EVENT and its 30 min at 1100 °C left out of the simulated heat; written as a RUN it stays as about 70 nm of oxide under the real one. `ETCH REMOVE ALL` (or `ETCH TO 0 nm`) would let the strip be simulated and the heat kept. *([Kar, Shanker and Chari 1985](/writing/interface-study-kar-1985))*
- **Which RUN is the oxidation.** The trap-density program takes the oxidation temperature from the first dry-oxygen RUN. A sacrificial oxidation in front of the real one changes the predicted density by a factor of 2.7 (4.3 to 1.6 × 10¹¹) through that choice alone. A `ROLE sacrificial|oxidation|anneal|pull` on each RUN would let programs find the oxidation by what it is (the same gap Hung 1987 hit with a boat-in). *([Kar, Shanker and Chari 1985](/writing/interface-study-kar-1985))*
- **A measured thickness as a constraint on an unstated time.** The paper states thicknesses, not times. Here the time was set by hand from the thickness and thickness was then dropped from the score, so the search could double the time unchecked. A sample field the alignment reads as a constraint (`OXIDE_NM_MEASURED` checked against the growth program while other quantities are searched) would pin the time and say so. *([Kar, Shanker and Chari 1985](/writing/interface-study-kar-1985))*
- **A band-edge peak as an observable.** Every number in Figure 2 is the height of a peak near Ev or Ec of an unannealed distribution. The observable vocabulary has midgap density and, after hydrogen only, a fixed set of energies. An observable `Dit_peak_near_Ev` / `Dit_peak_near_Ec` with its energy, and a program that predicts a distribution without hydrogen, are needed before any of the 18 peak values can be compared. *([Kar, Shanker and Chari 1985](/writing/interface-study-kar-1985))*
- **The clean.** “Degreasing in hot solvents, ultrasonic cleaning, and etching in acids” followed by a sacrificial oxide has no CLEAN word in the vocabulary; it is written `not_stated`. A `CLEAN: sacrificial_oxide_HF` would record the most consequential part of it. *([Kar, Shanker and Chari 1985](/writing/interface-study-kar-1985))*
- **How the measurement was made.** The densities are from illuminated admittance (capacitance and conductance, 30 Hz to 100 kHz) on 100 Å semitransparent Au or Al dots. Nothing in a history or result says which technique gave a density, and techniques disagree near the band edges; an observation statement with the method would let results from different methods be kept apart. *([Kar, Shanker and Chari 1985](/writing/interface-study-kar-1985))*
- **A freezing point that is stated and testable.** The as-grown series is the cleanest test of where the oxygen exchange stops: ten growth temperatures, one pull. With the stated hypothesis at 350 °C a realistic cool erases the growth temperature; at 450 °C it does not. The ontology could carry the freeze-out temperature of each operator as a declared hypothesis with its own test set (this series and Deal and Razouk's pulls), so that raising it is a recorded decision, not a template edit. *([Akinwande, Ho and Plummer 1981](/writing/interface-study-stanford-1981))*
- **The gas a wafer cools in.** A fast pull leaves the oxidation gas for a flushed mouth and then room air. The best variant here (cooling in nitrogen) is a Python edit; a PROFILE or WITHDRAW statement that names the gas after withdrawal would make it a declared unknown (`VARY ambient`). *([Akinwande, Ho and Plummer 1981](/writing/interface-study-stanford-1981))*
- **A starting charge from the laboratory.** The program's as-grown value is Deal's Fairchild line. `INITIAL Q_f FROM <laboratory line>` would let Stanford's own as-grown line (this report's Figure 7.7) be the start for Stanford's wafers, and make the Fairchild line one stated choice. *([Akinwande, Ho and Plummer 1981](/writing/interface-study-stanford-1981))*
- **A target observed on a fixed time grid, not a history.** The argon anneal times were “adjusted at each temperature to reach an equilibrium value” (1983 report). The language can only write a guessed duration. `RUN … UNTIL steady` (an anneal that lasts until the state stops moving) would state what the authors did and make the anneal time a program output instead of an assumption. *([Akinwande, Ho and Plummer 1981](/writing/interface-study-stanford-1981))*
- **One wafer measured between anneals.** The cycling is one sequence with a C-V after each step; it is written as five histories. A MEASURE event inside one history whose readings are the scored values would say it once, and would show that metal must come off between steps. *([Akinwande, Ho and Plummer 1981](/writing/interface-study-stanford-1981))*
- **Oxidation rate as a sample-history quantity.** Eq. 7.1 makes the as-grown charge a function of dx/dt at the end of growth. The growth programs compute it; the charge program cannot read another program's output. A cross-program QUANTITY (the oxidation rate at the pull) would let a rate-dependent charge law be written and tested on Figure 7.7. *([Akinwande, Ho and Plummer 1981](/writing/interface-study-stanford-1981))*
